question: After the death of Muhammad Ghori in 1206, who declared independence and founded the Slave dynasty of Delhi?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Qutbuddin Aibak.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Qutbuddin Aibak was Ghori's trusted slave-general in India; when Ghori died in 1206 he cut all ties with Ghori's kingdom and declared himself independent, thereby founding both the Slave (Mamluk/Ilbari) dynasty and the Delhi Sultanate (दिल्ली सल्तनत की स्थापना — कुतुबुद्दीन ऐबक, 1206)

 

• His reign lasted only four years, 1206-1210, and his capital was Lahore, not Delhi.

 

• He died suddenly in 1210 while playing chaugan (horse polo) at Lahore, where his tomb stands.

 

• He began the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque at Delhi, the Adhai-din-ka-Jhonpra at Ajmer and laid the foundation of the Qutub Minar.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The dynasty is also called the Mamluk dynasty, because 'mamluk' is the Quranic word for slave, and the Ilbari Turk dynasty.

 

• Aibak's successor was his son Aram Shah, who lasted about eight months before Iltutmish removed him.

 

• Aibak had earlier been Ghori's viceroy in India after the Second Battle of Tarain (1192).

 

• Dynasty period: 1206-1290, with the later Slave rulers ending in Kaiqubad.

 

NOTE

 

• Shamsuddin Iltutmish (Option 1): Iltutmish was Aibak's slave and son-in-law who took the throne in 1211 and made Delhi the capital; he strengthened the Sultanate but was not its founder.

 

• Ghiyasuddin Balban (Option 2): Balban ruled much later, from 1266 to 1287, and is remembered for the blood-and-iron policy and the destruction of the Forty; he was nowhere near the dawn of the Sultanate.

 

• Aram Shah (Option 4): Aram Shah was Aibak's son who held the throne for about eight months in 1210-11 before being defeated by Iltutmish, so he continued rather than founded the dynasty.

question: Which Delhi Sultan is regarded as the real founder of the Delhi Sultanate because he made Delhi his capital and gave the state its administrative shape?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Iltutmish.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Iltutmish (1211-36) was the Ilbari Turk noble who shifted the seat of power to Delhi and built the real administrative and political set-up of the Sultanate (दिल्ली सल्तनत का वास्तविक संस्थापक — इल्तुतमिश)

 

• He was sold as a slave by his half-brothers and bought by Aibak, who later gave him his daughter in marriage; hence he was called the 'slave of a slave'.

 

• He defeated Aram Shah in 1211, crushed rivals such as Yaldauz and Qabacha, and received formal recognition from the Caliph of Baghdad.

 

• He organised the iqta system, the Turkan-i-Chahalgani and issued the silver tanka and copper jital.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Aibak is only the first ruler of the Sultanate; Lahore, not Delhi, remained his capital throughout.

 

• Iltutmish's tomb at Delhi (near the Qutub complex) is one of the earliest Islamic tombs of India, and his era is called the Era of Tombs.

 

• He passed the throne by nomination to his daughter Raziya, which began hereditary succession in the Sultanate.

 

• He completed the Qutub Minar left unfinished by Aibak.

 

NOTE

 

• Qutbuddin Aibak (Option 2): Aibak founded the Sultanate in 1206 but never shifted his seat from Lahore and his four-year reign left little time for any administrative system.

 

• Balban (Option 3): Balban came three decades after Iltutmish and is known for kingship theory and strict court ceremony rather than creating the capital or the basic institutions of the Sultanate.

 

• Alauddin Khalji (Option 4): Alauddin Khalji belongs to the Khalji dynasty of the late thirteenth century; he built on an existing Delhi-based state and is known for market and army reforms.

question: The silver tanka (about 175 grains) and the copper jital were the standard coins issued by which Sultan?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Iltutmish.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Iltutmish introduced the purely Arabic-style coinage of the Sultanate: the silver tanka weighing about 175 grains and the copper jital (इल्तुतमिश के सिक्के — चाँदी का टंका, ताँबे का जीतल)

 

• These two coins became the basis of later Sultanate currency and show his effort to stabilise the monetary system after taking power at Delhi.

 

• The tanka was minted at several centres and carried the name of the Abbasid Caliph after Iltutmish obtained investiture in 1229.

 

• He is also credited with starting the iqta system of revenue assignments.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The jital remained in use for centuries and the tanka was the forerunner of the later rupee.

 

• Muhammad bin Tughlaq experimented with a token currency of copper in 1329-30, which is a different, later monetary measure.

 

• Iltutmish's tomb at Delhi and the Sultan Ghari tomb (built for his eldest son) show his building activity.

 

• Sher Shah Suri later issued the silver rupee of about 178 grains.

 

NOTE

 

• Alauddin Khalji (Option 1): Alauddin Khalji is known for cash salaries, price control and army reforms; his currency policy did not create the tanka and jital standard that predates his reign.

 

• Qutbuddin Aibak (Option 2): Aibak ruled only four years from Lahore, and the standardised silver tanka with the copper jital is credited to his son-in-law and successor rather than to him.

 

• Firoz Shah Tughlaq (Option 3): Firoz Shah Tughlaq issued mixed-metal coins such as the adha and bikh, but the original tanka and jital standard was set well before his time in the thirteenth century.

question: Which governor of Bhatinda revolted against Raziya Sultan and later married her?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Altunia.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Altunia was the iqtadar (governor) of Bhatinda who rose in revolt against Raziya; after he captured her, she married him to save her position (रज़िया सुल्ताना — भटिंडा का गवर्नर अल्तूनिया)

 

• Raziya (1236-40) was the first and only woman Sultan of Delhi, chosen by the people of Delhi after the nobles rejected her brother Ruknuddin Firoz.

 

• The couple marched towards Delhi but were killed at Kaithal in Haryana in 1240.

 

• She rejected the purdah system, wore the *kuba* and *kulah* and held open court.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Minhaj-us-Siraj, author of Tabaqat-i-Nasiri, admitted that Raziya was more capable than her brothers.

 

• Her reign of roughly four years ended in 1240 and was followed by weak rulers under the sway of the Forty.

 

• Iltutmish had nominated her as heir, the first instance of hereditary succession in the Sultanate.

 

• Her favourite Jamaluddin Yaqut, an Abyssinian, was disliked by the Turkish nobles.

 

NOTE

 

• Tajuddin Yaldauz (Option 1): Tajuddin Yaldauz was the ruler of Ghazni whom Iltutmish defeated around 1215-16 in the Tarain region; he lived a generation before Raziya's reign and never governed Bhatinda.

 

• Jamaluddin Yaqut (Option 3): Jamaluddin Yaqut was an Abyssinian officer promoted by Raziya as Master of the Horse; the Turkish nobles resented his rise, but he was not the Bhatinda governor who married her.

 

• Malik Kafur (Option 4): Malik Kafur was a slave-general of Alauddin Khalji who led southern campaigns in the early fourteenth century, long after Raziya's death in 1240.

question: Which Delhi Sultan introduced the Persian court customs of Sijda (prostration) and Paibos (kissing the Sultan's feet) and took the title Zill-i-Ilahi?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ghiyasuddin Balban.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ghiyasuddin Balban raised the prestige of the crown by calling himself Zill-i-Ilahi (shadow of God) and enforcing Sijda and Paibos at court, both Iranian ceremonies (बलबन — सिजदा और पाइबोस, ज़िल्ले-इलाही)

 

• He wanted to prove his superiority over the Turkish nobles known as the Forty, whom he was determined to crush.

 

• He also introduced the Persian festival Navroz in the court.

 

• His kingship theory was joined with the blood and iron policy, a ruthless approach to enemies of the throne.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Balban's full name was Ghiyasuddin Balban and he was also called Ulugh Khan; he ruled 1266-87.

 

• He reorganised the spy system and banned public sale of liquor and drugs.

 

• Diwan-i-Arz, the military department, is linked with him.

 

• Amir Khusro was a court poet under him, and his grandson Kaiqubad succeeded him.

 

NOTE

 

• Iltutmish (Option 2): Iltutmish was recognised by the Caliph of Baghdad and relied on the Turkish nobles; he did not enforce prostration or foot-kissing or claim to be the shadow of God.

 

• Alauddin Khalji (Option 3): Alauddin Khalji claimed great authority and called himself Sikandar-i-Sani, but the Sijda and Paibos ceremonies are specifically credited to Balban in the standard account of Sultanate court etiquette.

 

• Firoz Shah Tughlaq (Option 4): Firoz Shah Tughlaq governed according to the advice of the ulema and was known for public works and welfare departments, not for introducing Iranian court ceremonial.

question: In 1296, at which place did Alauddin Khalji treacherously murder his uncle and father-in-law Jalaluddin Khalji and seize the throne?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kara.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Alauddin returned from his raid on Devagiri to Kara, where he was the governor, and during the reception for the Sultan there he had Jalaluddin Khalji killed (कड़ा में जलालुद्दीन खिलजी की हत्या — 1296)

 

• Jalaluddin Firoz Khalji had founded the Khalji dynasty in 1290, ending the Slave rule after he killed Kaiqubad's young son.

 

• Alauddin's original name was Ali Gurshasp, and he was nephew and son-in-law of Jalaluddin.

 

• After the murder he marched to Delhi and took the throne, ruling from 1296 to 1316.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Alauddin was a Khalji noble first posted in the Kara-Manikpur region of present-day Uttar Pradesh before he became Sultan.

 

• Devagiri, the Yadava capital, was the target of his daring 1296 raid, which gave him wealth to win over nobles.

 

• Khalji period: 1290-1320, with Jalaluddin, Alauddin and the weak successors ending with Khusrau Khan.

 

• Alauddin later built his capital at Siri near Delhi.

 

NOTE

 

• Devagiri (Option 1): Devagiri was the place Alauddin had just raided and looted in 1296; he returned from it with great wealth but the murder did not occur there.

 

• Multan (Option 2): Multan was a frontier province for Mongol defence and a later governorship under Khizr Khan; it has no link with the killing of Jalaluddin Khalji.

 

• Lahore (Option 3): Lahore was Aibak's capital and a base against Mongols; Jalaluddin was not killed there, as the murder took place at Alauddin's own governorship of Kara.

question: In Alauddin Khalji's market control system in Delhi, each market was supervised by an officer called
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shahna-i-Mandi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Each of the four markets of Delhi was placed under a high officer called the Shahna-i-Mandi, who enforced the fixed prices (दिल्ली के बाज़ार का अधीक्षक — शहना-ए-मंडी)

 

• Alauddin set up separate markets for grain (Mandi), for cloth, sugar, dried fruits, butter and oil (Sarai-i-Adl), for horses, slaves and cattle, and for miscellaneous goods.

 

• Above these officers was the department Diwan-i-Riyasat, controlled by the Naib-i-Riyasat.

 

• The aim was to keep prices low so that a large army could live on cash salaries.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Banjaras were used to carry grain from villages to the city markets, and black marketing was strictly punished.

 

• A separate department, Diwan-i-Mustakhraj, handled arrears of revenue.

 

• Soldiers were controlled through the Dagh (branding of horses) and Huliya (descriptive roll).

 

• Alauddin's price list was fixed for essential commodities and enforced through spies.

 

NOTE

 

• Naib-i-Riyasat (Option 2): The Naib-i-Riyasat headed the Diwan-i-Riyasat, the central market department, and so ranked above individual market superintendents rather than being the officer of each market.

 

• Barid-i-Mamalik (Option 3): Barid-i-Mamalik was the head of the intelligence and news service of the empire, a post concerned with reporting from provinces, not with fixing prices in a market.

 

• Muqti (Option 4): A Muqti was the holder of an iqta, who led troops, kept order and collected revenue in his assigned territory; it was a provincial revenue and military post unrelated to the market system.

question: Malik Kafur, the general of Alauddin Khalji who led campaigns in South India, was bought as a slave at the time of the Gujarat expedition and was popularly known as
solution_text:
The correct answer is Hazar Dinari.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Malik Kafur was purchased for a thousand dinars during the Gujarat expedition (1299) and so came to be called Hazar Dinari; Alauddin later made him Malik Naib, the chief military commander (हज़ार दीनारी — मलिक काफूर)

 

• The Gujarat attack, the first after Alauddin became Sultan, was led by Nusrat Khan and Ulugh Khan.

 

• Under Malik Kafur the Sultanate armies went against Devagiri, Warangal and Madurai.

 

• He did not go against Vijayanagara, which was founded only in 1336.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Malik Kafur gained so much influence that after Alauddin's death in 1316 he dominated the court for a short time.

 

• Alauddin's southern campaigns brought rich booty from the Yadavas, Kakatiyas, Hoysalas and Pandyas.

 

• Gujarat's ruler at the time was the Vaghela king Karna, and Kafur is said to have been captured with the booty there.

 

• Alauddin died in 1316 and his tomb is in the Qutub complex, Delhi.

 

NOTE

 

• Khan-i-Jahan (Option 1): Khan-i-Jahan was the title of Firoz Shah Tughlaq's long-serving wazir, Maqbul, and is unconnected with the slave bought in Gujarat in Alauddin's reign.

 

• Zafar Khan (Option 3): Zafar Khan was a distinguished general of Alauddin who fought the Mongols and died in battle; he was a noble officer, not the slave purchased for a thousand dinars.

 

• Nusrat Khan (Option 4): Nusrat Khan was a senior Khalji commander who, with Ulugh Khan, led the Gujarat attack; he was the buyer's side, not the slave who got the thousand-dinar nickname.

question: During the siege of Chittor (1303), Alauddin Khalji fought the ruler Ratan Singh. Who composed the epic Padmavat based on the story of Padmavati?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Malik Muhammad Jayasi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Malik Muhammad Jayasi, a Sufi poet of Awadhi, composed Padmavat, which tells the story of Rani Padmavati, wife of Ratan Singh of Chittor (पद्मावत — मलिक मुहम्मद जायसी)

 

• Alauddin took Chittor in 1303, and the fort was renamed Khizrabad after his son Khizr Khan.

 

• Amir Khusro accompanied Alauddin in the campaign and described it in his own work.

 

• The poem is a literary retelling written centuries after the event, so historians treat it as a legend-based work.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Padmavat was composed around 1540 in Awadhi, during the early Sher Shah era, and belongs to the Sufi premakhyan tradition.

 

• Chittor was the Guhila (Sisodia line) kingdom of Mewar.

 

• Alauddin later built a new city at Siri and constructed the Alai Darwaza.

 

• Alauddin's southern conquests were mostly carried out by Malik Kafur.

 

NOTE

 

• Amir Khusro (Option 2): Amir Khusro was Alauddin's court poet who accompanied the army to Chittor and recorded events in Persian; the Awadhi epic Padmavat is not his work.

 

• Ziauddin Barani (Option 3): Ziauddin Barani authored Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi, a chronicle covering Balban to Firoz Shah; he did not compose any poetic epic on Padmavati.

 

• Minhaj-us-Siraj (Option 4): Minhaj-us-Siraj authored Tabaqat-i-Nasiri, which covers the period up to the mid-thirteenth century, so it predates Alauddin's Chittor campaign and has nothing about Padmavati.

question: Ibn Battuta, who reached the court of Muhammad bin Tughlaq in 1333, was later sent by the Sultan as his envoy to
solution_text:
The correct answer is China.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta was appointed a qazi at Delhi and was then sent as Muhammad bin Tughlaq's envoy to the Mongol ruler of China (मुहम्मद बिन तुग़लक़ का चीन दूत — इब्न बतूता)

 

• His travel account is the Kitab-ur-Rehla.

 

• He reported that the Sultan had conquered almost the whole of India, except Kashmir, Baluchistan and Rajputana.

 

• He described how local Hindu chieftains fortified themselves in dense bamboo groves.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ibn Battuta left Tangier in 1325 and spent several years in India before travelling on to China and the Maldives.

 

• He opined that Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's death was arranged by his son and the saint Nizamuddin Auliya.

 

• Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi by Ziauddin Barani is the other major source for the Tughlaq period.

 

• Muhammad bin Tughlaq ruled from 1325 to 1351.

 

NOTE

 

• Persia (Option 1): Persia was not the destination of the mission: Ibn Battuta had come from the Islamic lands and the Sultan's diplomatic gesture was directed to the Yuan court far to the east.

 

• Egypt (Option 2): Egypt, home of the Mamluk rulers and the Caliph, lay on the route Ibn Battuta had already travelled; it was not the place the Sultan sent him as ambassador.

 

• Khurasan (Option 4): Khurasan was the target of the Sultan's planned military expedition of 1339-40, a different matter altogether, and not the place to which Ibn Battuta went as an envoy.

question: Muhammad bin Tughlaq set up a new department, Diwan-i-Amir Kohi, in order to
option_4: provide marriage grants to poor girls
solution_text:
The correct answer is promote agriculture and extend cultivation.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Diwan-i-Amir Kohi was created by Muhammad bin Tughlaq to improve agriculture, mainly by bringing more land under cultivation (कृषि विभाग — दीवान-ए-अमीर कोही)

 

• The experiment was among his ambitious schemes, but it was poorly executed and gave poor results.

 

• It formed one of his five projects that failed, which also included the transfer of the capital (1327), token currency (1329), Doab taxation and the Khurasan expedition (1339-40).

 

• He was criticised because his schemes were too far ahead of the administrative capacity of his time.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Muhammad bin Tughlaq's original name was Juna (Jauna) Khan, and he was crowned at Delhi in 1325.

 

• The Doab tax increase coincided with a severe famine and caused peasant flight and revolt.

 

• Barani's Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi gives a harsh account of his schemes.

 

• He appointed people from humble professions to high administrative posts.

 

NOTE

 

• collect arrears of revenue (Option 2): Arrears of revenue were handled by Alauddin Khalji's Diwan-i-Mustakhraj, a separate department established to check corruption among revenue officials and collect dues.

 

• recruit and inspect soldiers (Option 3): Recruitment and inspection of soldiers were the business of the Diwan-i-Arz, linked with Balban, which was the military department of the Sultanate.

 

• provide marriage grants to poor girls (Option 4): Marriage help for poor girls and widows came from the Diwan-i-Khairat, established later by Firoz Shah Tughlaq and not by Muhammad bin Tughlaq.

question: Who was appointed governor of Multan by Timur before he left India and later captured Delhi to found the Sayyid dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Khizr Khan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Khizr Khan was left by Timur as governor of Multan; he then captured Delhi in 1414 and became the founder of the Sayyid dynasty (सैयद वंश का संस्थापक — खिज्र खाँ)

 

• Timur had invaded in 1398, defeated Nasiruddin Mahmud Tughlaq's forces and sacked Delhi for three days, withdrawing in 1399.

 

• His invasion gave a death-blow to the Tughlaq dynasty and left the Sultanate fragmented.

 

• Khizr Khan ruled 1414-21 and did not take the title of Sultan, acknowledging Timur's house.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Sayyid dynasty ruled from 1414 to 1451 with four rulers: Khizr Khan, Mubarak Shah, Muhammad Shah and Alauddin Alam Shah.

 

• Alam Shah ended it by giving up the throne to Bahlol Lodi.

 

• Timur's invasion is chronicled as a turning point of the Tughlaq decline.

 

• The Sayyids claimed descent from the Prophet and ruled mostly a small area around Delhi.

 

NOTE

 

• Bahlol Lodi (Option 1): Bahlol Lodi was governor of Sirhind and Lahore who became Sultan in 1451 after the last Sayyid abdicated; he was not Timur's appointee and he founded a different dynasty.

 

• Daulat Khan Lodi (Option 2): Daulat Khan Lodi was an Afghan noble who ruled the Delhi throne briefly in 1412-14 and was defeated by Khizr Khan; he was not appointed governor by Timur.

 

• Mubarak Shah (Option 3): Mubarak Shah was Khizr Khan's son and successor in 1421, so he was a Sayyid ruler but not the one who held Multan under Timur's authority.

question: Who was the first Sultan of Delhi to be killed on a battlefield?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ibrahim Lodi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ibrahim Lodi, the last Sultan of the Lodi dynasty, was killed fighting Babur at the First Battle of Panipat (1526), the first Delhi Sultan to die in battle (प्रथम पानीपत युद्ध — इब्राहिम लोदी मारा गया)

 

• The defeat ended the Delhi Sultanate and opened the way for the Mughal empire.

 

• Gunpowder and artillery were used for the first time in a major battle in India, and Babur used the Ottoman tactic of *tulughma* and *araba*.

 

• Ibrahim ruled 1517-26 and had antagonised Afghan nobles, including Daulat Khan Lodi and Alam Khan.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Panipat also marks the end of the five dynasties of the Sultanate: Slave, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi.

 

• Rana Sanga's rivalry with Ibrahim Lodi over eastern Rajasthan and Malwa also set the scene.

 

• Babur later fought Rana Sanga at Khanwa in 1527.

 

• The Lodi dynasty is the first Afghan dynasty to rule at Delhi.

 

NOTE

 

• Bahlol Lodi (Option 2): Bahlol Lodi died a natural death in 1489 after a long reign of nearly 38 years; he was the longest-serving sultan and his tomb stands at Delhi.

 

• Sikandar Lodi (Option 3): Sikandar Lodi died in 1517 of an illness (a throat disease according to chronicles) and was succeeded by Ibrahim; he was not killed in any battle.

 

• Muhammad bin Tughlaq (Option 4): Muhammad bin Tughlaq died in 1351 near Thatta in Sindh while chasing a rebel, reportedly of fever, so he did not fall on a battlefield.

question: Which poet of the Delhi Sultanate, known as the 'Parrot of India' (Tuti-i-Hind), served as court poet to several rulers and is credited with creating the sitar and tabla?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Amir Khusro.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Amir Khusro, born in Uttar Pradesh, was called the Parrot of India and served about eight rulers, from Balban to Muhammad bin Tughlaq (तूती-ए-हिन्द — अमीर खुसरो)

 

• Tradition credits him with inventing the sitar and tabla and with creating qawwali.

 

• He composed in Persian and also in Hindavi, and enjoyed Alauddin Khalji's patronage though the Sultan was himself illiterate.

 

• He was a disciple of the Chishti saint Nizamuddin Auliya.

 

• His name Khusro is linked with the Chishti saint Nizamuddin Auliya, whose disciple he was, and he composed verses in Persian as well as in the early Hindavi speech of the north.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Alauddin also patronised Amir Hasan, another poet of the court.

 

• Amir Khusro accompanied Alauddin on the Chittor campaign of 1303.

 

• Prose histories of the age are called tawarikh and were composed by administrators, secretaries, poets and courtiers.

 

• Khusro's Persian works include Khazain-ul-Futuh describing Alauddin's conquests.

 

• Amir Khusro's Persian prose and verse also record the conquests of Alauddin Khalji, and he is said to have contributed to the blend of Persian and Indian music.

 

NOTE

 

• Amir Hasan Sijzi (Option 1): Amir Hasan was a poet of Alauddin's court and a friend of Khusro, but the epithet Parrot of India and the credit for sitar and tabla go to Khusro, not to him.

 

• Ziauddin Barani (Option 3): Ziauddin Barani was a historian, not a musician or poet, whose Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi records the political events from Balban to the early Firoz Shah period.

 

• Minhaj-us-Siraj (Option 4): Minhaj-us-Siraj was the thirteenth-century chronicler of Tabaqat-i-Nasiri and a judge; he was a historian and had no connection with the sitar, tabla or the epithet.

question: After Qutbuddin Aibak built the first storey of the Qutub Minar, who added three more storeys to it?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Iltutmish.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Iltutmish added three more storeys to the Minar that Aibak had started as a victory tower and carried up to the first storey (क़ुतुब मीनार — ऐबक ने शुरू किया, इल्तुतमिश ने पूरा किया)

 

• The first three floors are of red sandstone; the fourth and fifth are of grey sandstone and white marble.

 

• Firoz Shah Tughlaq rebuilt the fourth storey after lightning damage and added the fifth.

 

• The tower tapers from about 14.32 m at the base to about 2.75 m at the top and is about 73 m tall.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• It is the tallest brick minaret in the world and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

 

• Alauddin Khalji added the Alai Darwaza, the southern gate of the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, and began the unfinished Alai Minar.

 

• Sikandar Lodi also repaired the Minar.

 

• Tradition names the Minar after the Sufi saint Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki.

 

NOTE

 

• Alauddin Khalji (Option 1): Alauddin Khalji added the Alai Darwaza in the Qutub complex and began a larger Alai Minar, but his additions do not form the second to fourth storeys of the Qutub Minar.

 

• Balban (Option 2): Balban's building work is associated with the Lal Mahal and an Islamic-style tomb, not with raising any storey of the Qutub Minar.

 

• Firoz Shah Tughlaq (Option 3): Firoz Shah Tughlaq reconstructed the fourth storey after lightning damaged it and added the fifth, so his work came well after the three storeys added in the thirteenth century.

question: The last Sayyid ruler, Alauddin Alam Shah, gave up the throne in 1451 in favour of
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bahlol Lodi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Alauddin Alam Shah (1445-51), the last ruler of the Sayyid line, voluntarily gave up his throne to Bahlol Lodi, who founded the Lodi dynasty (अलाउद्दीन आलम शाह — बहलोल लोदी को सत्ता सौंपी, 1451)

 

• Bahlol thus began the first Afghan dynasty to rule at Delhi, lasting 1451-1526.

 

• He ruled for about 38 years, the longest reign among the Delhi Sultans.

 

• He avoided the throne and sat on a carpet along with his Afghan amirs, treating them as equals.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• His tomb lies in Delhi, and his son Sikandar succeeded him in 1489.

 

• Alam Shah is said to have preferred a quiet life at Badaun after his abdication.

 

• The five dynasties of the Sultanate were Slave (1206-90), Khalji (1290-1320), Tughlaq (1320-1414), Sayyid (1414-51) and Lodi (1451-1526).

 

• The Sayyids had earlier been established by Khizr Khan after Timur's invasion.

 

NOTE

 

• Sikandar Lodi (Option 1): Sikandar Lodi was Bahlol's son who came to the throne only in 1489, after his father's death, and he is known for founding Agra in 1504 rather than for receiving a throne from Alam Shah.

 

• Daulat Khan Lodi (Option 2): Daulat Khan Lodi had been an earlier governor who held Delhi briefly after Mahmud Tughlaq (1412-14) and was removed by Khizr Khan, so he stands in a different transition altogether.

 

• Khizr Khan (Option 4): Khizr Khan founded the Sayyid line in 1414 and is therefore the first ruler of the dynasty, not the one who surrendered it in 1451.

question: In the Delhi Sultanate, what was the main duty of a Muqti in his assigned iqta?
option_1: to lead military campaigns, maintain law and order and collect revenue
option_2: to build forts and mosques in the Sultan's name
option_3: to look after the royal stables and import horses
option_4: to lead the royal court and decide religious matters
solution_text:
The correct answer is to lead military campaigns, maintain law and order and collect revenue.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A Muqti (iqtadar) held an iqta, a revenue assignment given in place of salary, and was expected to lead military campaigns, maintain law and order and collect revenue (मुक्ती — इक़्ता का धारक)

 

• From the collected revenue he paid his troops and sent the surplus to the Sultan's treasury.

 

• The iqta system is associated with Iltutmish, and iqtadars were transferable from time to time.

 

• The post was made hereditary under Firoz Shah Tughlaq.

 

• The collected surplus was meant to flow upward: the Muqti first met the cost of his soldiers and administration, and the balance went to the Sultan, which made iqtas a link between local control and the central treasury.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Land held directly by the king was khalsa land, while iqta lands were assigned to soldiers, officers and nobles.

 

• Alauddin Khalji preferred cash salaries for the regular army, so iqta's military role was reduced for his troops.

 

• The word iqta means a revenue assignment, not a province in the sense of a fixed political unit.

 

• Mansabdars were a Mughal-period rank holders, not Sultanate officers.

 

NOTE

 

• to build forts and mosques in the Sultan's name (Option 2): Construction of forts and mosques was the work of royal builders and public works officials, not the main task of a revenue assignee; Firoz Shah's PWD was separate.

 

• to look after the royal stables and import horses (Option 3): Stable management and the import of horses were matters for the royal military establishment and traders, and had nothing to do with administering an iqta.

 

• to lead the royal court and decide religious matters (Option 4): Court leadership and religious rulings were handled by the Sultan with ulema and qazis; a Muqti was a territorial official whose job was provincial control.

question: In Delhi Sultanate taxation, which levy gave the Sultan one-fifth of the loot taken in war?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Khums.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Khums (Khams) was the one-fifth share of the plunder of war that went to the Sultan, the remainder being distributed among the army (खम्स — युद्ध में लूट का पाँचवाँ भाग)

 

• It was a tax on war booty, so its income depended on the success of campaigns.

 

• In the Islamic fiscal scheme it ranked beside zakat and jizya as an established category of public revenue.

 

• The Sultanate levied it on treasure and spoils taken from defeated enemies.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Zakat was a religious tax on Muslims, taken at about 2-2.5 per cent of property.

 

• Jizya was the religious tax on non-Muslims; Firoz Shah Tughlaq was the first Delhi Sultan to impose it on Brahmins also.

 

• Kharaj was a land tax, mostly collected from non-Muslim cultivators.

 

• Usher was a levy of 5-10 per cent on Muslims' produce.

 

NOTE

 

• Zakat (Option 1): Zakat was a religious tax paid by Muslims on their wealth at a low rate of about two to two and a half per cent, and has no link with war booty.

 

• Jizya (Option 2): Jizya was a poll-type tax charged on non-Muslim subjects in return for security and exemption from military service, so it was not a share of war plunder.

 

• Kharaj (Option 4): Kharaj was a land revenue levied on cultivators and mostly on non-Muslims, collected from produce of the soil rather than from plunder taken in battle.

question: "A king cannot survive without soldiers, and soldiers cannot survive without salary." Which author emphasised this in the context of the thirteenth-century Delhi Sultanate?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Fakhr-i Mudabbir.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Fakhr-i Mudabbir, in his work Adab-ul-Harb wa'sh-Shuja'a, argued that soldiers need salaries, salaries come from revenue, revenue comes from peasants, and peasants can pay only when prosperous and safe under the king (फ़ख़्र-ए-मुदब्बिर — आदाब-उल-हरब)

 

• The chain of logic links the army, finance and agriculture.

 

• He lived in the thirteenth-century Sultanate, during the Slave period, when the state was building its military machinery.

 

• The idea anticipates the later cash-salary policy of Alauddin Khalji.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Alauddin's market control was designed so that his huge standing army could survive on moderate salaries.

 

• Iltutmish's iqta system paid soldiers through land assignments instead of cash.

 

• The Persian word Bandagan denoted military slaves purchased by the Sultan.

 

• Tawarikh authors included secretaries, administrators, poets and courtiers.

 

• Adab-ul-Harb wa'sh-Shuja'a was composed in the early thirteenth century and dedicated to Iltutmish, and it discusses war, soldiers and kingship.

 

NOTE

 

• Minhaj-us-Siraj (Option 2): Minhaj-us-Siraj authored Tabaqat-i-Nasiri, a general history that praised Raziya's ability; it is not the work in which the soldier-salary-peasant chain is set out.

 

• Ziauddin Barani (Option 3): Ziauddin Barani lived in the fourteenth century and authored Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi; the question refers to a thirteenth-century political thinker.

 

• Ibn Battuta (Option 4): Ibn Battuta was a traveller of the fourteenth century whose Rihla records observations of places and customs, not a theory of the king, army and revenue.

question: What did the Persian term 'Bandagan' refer to in the early Delhi Sultanate?
option_1: Landed chieftains who served as governors
option_2: Military slaves purchased by the Sultan
option_3: Religious scholars attached to the court
option_4: Officers who measured land for revenue
solution_text:
The correct answer is Military slaves purchased by the Sultan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Bandagan was the Persian word for military slaves bought by the Sultan and trained to serve him loyally (बंदगान — सुल्तान द्वारा खरीदे गए सैन्य दास)

 

• The Slave dynasty drew its name from rulers like Aibak and Iltutmish who began as purchased slaves.

 

• Iltutmish, sold by his half-brothers, was bought by Aibak and then became his son-in-law.

 

• Such slaves often rose to high commands, and Alauddin's Malik Kafur, bought for a thousand dinars, is a later example.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Firoz Shah Tughlaq maintained a large department of slaves, the Diwan-i-Bandagan.

 

• The Slave dynasty is also called the Mamluk dynasty, mamluk being the Quranic word for slave.

 

• Slaves were valued because they depended on the Sultan alone and had no local ties.

 

• Balban, once a slave himself, rose to be Ulugh Khan before becoming Sultan.

 

NOTE

 

• Landed chieftains who served as governors (Option 1): Landed chieftains were local rulers or zamindars who were brought into the system as governors, a free hereditary class rather than slaves purchased for service.

 

• Religious scholars attached to the court (Option 3): Religious scholars were ulema, qazis and sufis who advised the Sultans on matters of faith and law; they were respected free men, not bought as soldiers, so the term for purchased military slaves cannot refer to them.

 

• Officers who measured land for revenue (Option 4): Land measurement officers were revenue staff; Alauddin's Biswa and Sikandar Lodi's Gaz were measurement units and had no link with the word Bandagan.

question:
Consider the following statements about Qutbuddin Aibak:

1. Lahore was his capital.

2. He died while playing chaugan (horse polo).

3. He completed all five storeys of the Qutub Minar.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Aibak ruled from Lahore and never made Delhi his capital (ऐबक — राजधानी लाहौर, चौगान में मृत्यु)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: he died suddenly in 1210 from an accident while playing chaugan, and he is buried at Lahore.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: he only began the Qutub Minar as a victory tower and raised it to the first storey; Iltutmish added three storeys and Firoz Shah Tughlaq rebuilt the fourth and added the fifth.

 

• So only statements 1 and 2 hold.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Aibak also built the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque at Delhi using material from demolished temples, and Adhai-din-ka-Jhonpra at Ajmer.

 

• His son Aram Shah succeeded him but was replaced by Iltutmish after about eight months.

 

• The Quwwat-ul-Islam is described as the first mosque built at Delhi by the Turks.

 

• Aibak's reign is 1206-1210.

 

NOTE

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 1): Pairing statement 2 with statement 3 wrongly accepts the claim that Aibak finished the Minar; he stopped at the first storey and later rulers completed it.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 2): Pairing statement 1 with statement 3 wrongly drops the correct polo-accident fact and accepts the false completion claim, so it is also incorrect.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Taking all three statements as true overlooks the fact that the Qutub Minar was a multi-ruler work finished long after Aibak's death in 1210.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Turkan-i-Chahalgani:

1. It was a group of forty powerful Turkish nobles formed by Iltutmish.

2. Balban broke its power although he had once been a member.

3. It was formed by Alauddin Khalji to control the Mongols.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Iltutmish organised the Turkan-i-Chahalgani (Group of Forty) of powerful Turkish nobles, partly to meet Mongol pressure (तुर्कान-ए-चहलगानी — इल्तुतमिश का चालीस सरदारों का दल)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: Balban, himself once among the Forty, saw them as the real danger to the monarchy and destroyed them.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: the Forty belonged to the thirteenth-century Slave era and were already gone by the time Alauddin Khalji came to power in 1296.

 

• Hence the combination of 1 and 2 only is correct.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The group effectively controlled the throne after Iltutmish and weakened his children, including Raziya.

 

• Balban's blood-and-iron policy and strict spy system were tools against nobles.

 

• He also introduced Sijda, Paibos and Zill-i-Ilahi to increase the Sultan's stature.

 

• Alauddin's four ordinances (confiscating properties, spy system, ban on liquor and social gatherings) dealt with nobles in a different way.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 (Option 1): Choosing statement 1 alone overlooks that Balban's destruction of the Forty, which is correct, is also a correct statement on this institution.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 2): Combining 2 with 3 accepts the false attribution to Alauddin Khalji; the group existed under Iltutmish, not under the Khaljis, and the Mongol link is only partly right.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Accepting all three statements includes the wrong claim that Alauddin Khalji created the Forty to counter the Mongols, whereas the group was Iltutmish's creation in the thirteenth century and had been destroyed long before 1296.

question:
Consider the following statements about the army reforms of Alauddin Khalji:

1. Dagh was the branding of horses.

2. Chehra/Huliya was a tax on grazing cattle.

3. Soldiers were paid regular cash salaries.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 3 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Dagh system meant branding of government horses to prevent fraud (अलाउद्दीन के सैन्य सुधार — दाग़ और हुलिया)

 

• Statement 2 is incorrect: Chehra/Huliya was a descriptive roll of soldiers; the grazing tax was Chari, which was levied on pastures along with the Ghari house tax.

 

• Statement 3 is correct: Alauddin built a large standing army paid in cash, which led directly to his market control policy.

 

• So the statements 1 and 3 hold together.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Regular review of the army was undertaken to maintain efficiency.

 

• Alauddin also confiscated nobles' properties and reorganised the spy system.

 

• He used Mongol-style discipline, and the army fought off Mongol invasions repeatedly.

 

• The descriptive roll is called Huliya in some sources and Chehra in others; both names denote the record of each soldier's appearance.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 3 (Option 1): Only 3 is wrong because it ignores Dagh, a well-established Alauddin measure for controlling the quality of cavalry horses and eliminating fraud in musters.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): Combining 2 and 3 accepts the false claim that Huliya was a grazing tax, which is actually the Chari levy, so the combination fails.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Taking all three as true includes the false identification of the descriptive roll as a tax on grazing cattle, when it recorded soldiers' physical details.

question:
Consider the following statements about Alauddin Khalji's market reforms:

1. Four separate markets were set up in Delhi.

2. The Diwan-i-Mustakhraj regulated the prices of goods.

3. The measures were intended to raise prices so that traders could earn more.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Delhi had four markets, for grain, for cloth-sugar-oil goods (Sarai-i-Adl), for horses-slaves-cattle and for miscellaneous goods (अलाउद्दीन की बाज़ार नियंत्रण नीति)

 

• Statement 2 is incorrect: price control rested with the Diwan-i-Riyasat under the Naib-i-Riyasat; the Diwan-i-Mustakhraj was the department that collected arrears of revenue and checked corruption.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: the purpose was to keep prices low so that the Sultan's large army could live on cash salaries.

 

• Hence only statement 1 is valid.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Each market was supervised by a Shahna-i-Mandi.

 

• Black marketing was strictly prohibited and a public distribution arrangement existed.

 

• Banjaras brought grain from villages to the markets.

 

• Alauddin also measured land using the Biswa as the unit.

 

• Alauddin's spies reported on prices and on the weights used by shopkeepers; traders who cheated customers were punished with cutting of flesh equal to the shortfall in weight.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 2 only (Option 1): Including statement 2 mistakes the revenue-arrears department for a price-regulation body; the Mustakhraj collected dues from officials, while price fixing lay with the Riyasat department.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 2): Combining 1 with 3 repeats the false idea that the aim was higher traders' earnings, when the aim was low prices for the military's sake.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): Pairing 2 and 3 is doubly wrong because neither the Mustakhraj nor a rise in prices had any role in the market control policy.

question:
Consider the following statements about Muhammad bin Tughlaq:

1. He shifted the capital from Delhi to Lahore in 1327.

2. He introduced a token currency in 1329.

3. Ibn Battuta visited his court in 1333.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2 and 3 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is incorrect: in 1327 he transferred the capital from Delhi to Devagiri, renamed Daulatabad, not to Lahore (मुहम्मद बिन तुग़लक़ — राजधानी परिवर्तन, सांकेतिक मुद्रा)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: in 1329 he issued a token currency of copper in place of silver, a plan that failed and damaged his prestige.

 

• Statement 3 is correct: the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta came to his court in 1333 and recorded his stay in the Kitab-ur-Rehla in the Kitab-ur-Rehla.

 

• So the correct combination is 2 and 3.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Doab tax increase, the Diwan-i-Amir Kohi and the Khurasan expedition were his other experiments.

 

• Twenty-seven revolts in the south were one reason cited for moving the capital.

 

• He ruled from 1325 to 1351 and his original name was Juna Khan (Ulugh Khan).

 

• Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi by Barani is a main source on his reign.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 2 only (Option 1): Linking 1 with 2 treats the move to Lahore as true; the Sultan moved to the Deccan town of Devagiri, which is in the south, far from Lahore.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 2): Combining 1 with 3 repeats the Lahore error while dropping the token currency, which is a well-documented measure of the year 1329.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Accepting all three statements repeats the incorrect capital destination from the first statement; the Sultan moved to Devagiri, renamed Daulatabad, in the Deccan, a very different place from Lahore.
